clue.text: Melville being the lady's husband

definitions.note: the first name of the novelist Herman Melville

blocks.note: the possessive pronoun for a woman
man as in 'man and wife'

explanation.surface: A biographical note that Melville was some woman's husband.
explanation.walkthrough: Melville is taken as a surname, but the answer is the novelist's first name; 'the lady's husband' is HER MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Herman Melville wrote Moby-Dick, so his forename is clued by naming his surname.

clue.text: Mysterious East cries to reveal such secrets

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing such secrets

indicators.note: something mysterious is obscure and jumbled, so the letters that follow are scrambled

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for East
taken as written

explanation.surface: Strange cries from the East seem to give away hidden secrets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mysterious' looks like the definition, but it is the signal to rearrange E with CRIES TO.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoteric knowledge is understood only by an inner circle of initiates, which describes secrets of that kind.

clue.text: Its iron tongue told twelve (M N Dream)

blocks.note: surface reading: a bell's clapper striking twelve
setter's reading: a quotation from A Midsummer Night's Dream naming an hour

explanation.surface: A church bell's iron clapper strikes twelve, as Shakespeare puts it.
explanation.walkthrough: Theseus says in A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act 5: 'The iron tongue of midnight hath told twelve.' The bracket gives the play's title in shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: In the quoted line the hour whose bell strikes twelve is the one ending the day.

clue.text: Mice sound disturbing to an old Pharisee

indicators.note: disturbing things knocks them out of place, so these letters are moved about

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The noise of mice is upsetting an elderly Pharisee.
explanation.definitionFit: In John's Gospel Nicodemus is a Pharisee who visits Jesus by night, a figure from the first century.

clue.text: Humble plea made at petrol pump, in highland dress for a spell?

definitions.text: Humble plea made at petrol pump

blocks.clueFragment: Humble plea made at petrol pump
blocks.note: first meaning: a polite request to an attendant, split as '...'
second meaning: the Scottish kilt

explanation.surface: A motorist politely asks to have the tank filled while wearing a kilt for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as three words, the answer is the request 'Fill, I beg'; 'for a spell' hints that the plea spells out the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A filibeg is an old Scots word for the short pleated kilt worn by Highlanders.

clue.text: Captain's record some aid to Berlin?

blocks.note: first meaning: the ship's daily journal kept by the master
second meaning: a berlin is a kind of carriage, and a vehicle's registration document was called by this name

explanation.surface: A ship captain's records were somehow of help to the city of Berlin.
explanation.walkthrough: Berlin is not the city here: a berlin is a four-wheeled carriage, and a UK car's registration document was long known by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ships keep a log recording each voyage, and British motorists held a similar registration document for their vehicle.

clue.text: Good health report of him and his wife Mary

blocks.clueFragment: Good health report of him and his wife
blocks.note: surface reading: news that a married couple are both fine
setter's reading: the 'him' is the third husband of Mary, Queen of Scots

explanation.surface: A bulletin saying a man and his wife Mary are in good health.
explanation.walkthrough: The health report is 'both well'; James Hepburn, Earl of Bothwell, married Mary Queen of Scots in 1567.
explanation.definitionFit: The Earl married the Scottish queen Mary, so he is the husband the clue's 'him' refers to.

clue.text: Make concession to broadcaster in Lincolnshire

definitions.note: names a town in Lincolnshire rather than giving a noun

blocks.note: to grant is to concede
a ham is an amateur radio broadcaster

explanation.surface: Giving way to a radio presenter somewhere in Lincolnshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincolnshire is an English county on the east coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Grantham is a market town in the English county, birthplace of Margaret Thatcher.

clue.text: After a nil bid, perhaps, exchanged ace for queen

indicators.note: things exchanged swap places, so the letters change their positions

blocks.note: taken as written
nil is zero, the letter O
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bridge player who bid nothing then swaps an ace for a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The card-table picture hides an anagram of A, O, BID and ACE.
explanation.definitionFit: Boadicea, also spelled Boudicca, was queen of the Iceni who led a revolt against Roman Britain.

clue.text: From time to time an apprentice would be needed for magazine

indicators.note: saying these letters would be needed means they are lacking from the longer word

blocks.note: a magazine is a regular publication
A for an, L for learner or apprentice

explanation.surface: Now and then a trainee would be required for a magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: PERIODIC needs AL added to become PERIODICAL, a magazine; the wordplay works backwards from the longer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something periodic recurs at intervals, happening occasionally rather than constantly.

clue.text: Bird dog retrieved with intelligence

indicators.note: something retrieved is brought back, so the word dog is read in the backward direction

blocks.note: taken as written
wit is mental sharpness

explanation.surface: A gun dog fetches a shot bird and shows its cleverness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retrieved' fits a gun dog fetching game, which hides its job of turning the word round.
explanation.definitionFit: The godwit is a long-billed wading bird of mudflats and marshes.

clue.text: How sad one felt in Keats's alien cornfield

definitions.text: How sad one felt in Keats's alien cornfield

blocks.note: surface reading: someone's sorrow
setter's reading: Ruth in the Ode to a Nightingale, 'sick for home' amid the alien corn

explanation.surface: Someone's sorrow while standing in a strange cornfield from a Keats poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's Ode to a Nightingale describes Ruth who, 'sick for home, she stood in tears amid the alien corn'; swap the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruth was longing for her native land, the feeling of missing one's family and house.

clue.text: Try to get fish - it's a sound skin-food

blocks.note: to have a crack at something is to try it
the ling is a cod-like sea fish

explanation.surface: An attempt at catching fish, followed by talk of a healthy food for the skin.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays two ways at once: the word is a snapping sound and also crisp roast pork rind.
explanation.definitionFit: Crackling is both a series of sharp snapping noises and the crisp roasted rind on pork, eaten as food.

clue.text: Ian returns to Civil Service

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way one came, so the following words are read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
CS is the abbreviation for Civil Service

explanation.surface: A man called Ian goes back to work in the Civil Service.
explanation.walkthrough: Ian is a typically Scottish name, so it stands as an example for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian is the Scottish form of John, so a man of that name typifies a native of Scotland.

clue.text: Start out for the service on the river

blocks.note: a service of crockery is a set
the Forth is a Scottish river

explanation.surface: Heading off to a church service held beside the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' suggests worship, but it is a dinner service, a set of dishes.
explanation.definitionFit: To set forth is to begin a journey, the same as setting off or departing.

clue.text: The table d'hote is not remarkable

blocks.note: first meaning: an old word for a fixed-price set meal at an inn
second meaning: plain, commonplace

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a diner's verdict on a set menu; the first meaning is an archaic noun for such a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordinary was a public meal served at a fixed price in a tavern, and the adjective means unexceptional.

clue.text: Severely criticize a very tricky feat

blocks.note: first meaning: to attack harshly in words
second meaning: in bridge, winning all or all but one of the tricks

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tricky' sounds like 'difficult' but means 'made of tricks': a bridge slam takes twelve or thirteen of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Critics slam a bad play, and in bridge a grand or small slam is taking nearly every trick.

clue.text: Formal display by draughtsman?

blocks.note: first meaning: an elaborately arranged show or scene
second meaning: a draughtsman is one counter from a draughts set

explanation.surface: A formal exhibition of drawings by a technical artist.
explanation.walkthrough: A draughtsman here is a counter in draughts, the British name for checkers, not someone who draws.
explanation.definitionFit: A set piece is a carefully staged display, and a draughts counter is literally one piece of the set.

clue.text: Transports emergency supplies - to Berlin?

blocks.note: surface reading: moving relief goods by any means
setter's reading: the 1948-49 operation flying food into blockaded West Berlin

explanation.surface: Relief supplies are being carried to the German capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark points to the Berlin blockade, when the Allies supplied the city entirely by aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means carrying goods or people by aircraft, especially in an emergency or blockade.

clue.text: Get away without a key - what a lark!

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the first word wraps around the others

blocks.note: to escape is to get away
taken as written
D is a musical key

explanation.surface: Fleeing without needing a key, someone treats it as great fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking', but here it means 'outside'; the letters A and D go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapade is a reckless adventure or prank, and a lark is a bit of mischievous fun.

clue.text: Opening the way to the drum?

definitions.text: Opening the way to the drum?

blocks.clueFragment: Opening the way to the drum?
blocks.note: surface reading: clearing a path to a percussion instrument
setter's reading: the eardrum, reached through an opening in the head

explanation.surface: Clearing a route to reach the drum kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' reads as a verb, but it is a noun: the passage leading in to the eardrum.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal name for the ear canal, the passage that leads inward to the tympanic membrane.

clue.text: A day's growth on a tree

blocks.note: setter's reading: a named day in the English calendar, 29 May, marking Charles II's restoration
surface reading: a day's worth of new growth on a tree

explanation.surface: How much a tree grows in a single day.
explanation.walkthrough: Oak Apple Day, 29 May, marked Charles II's restoration and recalled his hiding in an oak; the answer is also a gall on oak trees.
explanation.definitionFit: An oak apple is a round gall formed on oak twigs by wasp larvae, a growth on the tree.

clue.text: This is why shortly numbers are to be changed

indicators.note: letters that are to be changed must take a new order

blocks.note: NOS is the short form of numbers
taken as written

explanation.surface: An explanation for why the figures will soon be altered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' looks like 'soon', but it tells you to abbreviate numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: A reason is the cause or explanation behind something, what is given when asked why.

clue.text: Repellent thing for a golfer to do?

definitions.text: Repellent thing for a golfer to do?

blocks.note: setter's reading: the phrase means to repel or chase away
surface reading: a golfer's opening stroke from the tee

explanation.surface: Something disgusting that a golfer might do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repellent' reads as 'disgusting' but means 'repelling'; a golfer also begins each hole by hitting from the tee.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive off is to force attackers back, and also a golfer's first shot from the tee.

clue.text: Coward's complaint

blocks.note: surface reading: the grumble or ailment of a timid person
setter's reading: Noel Coward, the playwright, whose 1925 comedy is named after an ailment

explanation.surface: The grievance or illness of someone lacking courage.
explanation.walkthrough: Coward is Noel Coward, whose comedy of a weekend house party is titled after this allergy.
explanation.definitionFit: Hay Fever is a Coward play, and it is a complaint in the sense of an illness: pollen allergy.

clue.text: Slippery Greek midshipman?

blocks.note: GR is the abbreviation for Greek
Mr Midshipman Easy is the hero of a Captain Marryat novel

explanation.surface: An untrustworthy Greek junior naval officer.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Midshipman Easy is an 1836 sea novel by Frederick Marryat; the question mark flags that the officer is a fictional one.
explanation.definitionFit: Something covered in grease or oil is slick and hard to grip, hence slippery.
